newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian parliament debates cabinet resignation.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian parliament debates cabinet resignation.

text.p: Bulgaria's parliament on Saturday began debating the resignation of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov and his cabinet, tendered at a party congress a week ago.

Under fire for his handling of a severe economic crisis, Videnov resigned last Saturday, saying he felt he lacked the support he needed from the party and the country to continue as prime minister and party leader.
"The resignation of the cabinet allows parliament to choose the way which is best for the country," he told parliament.
Videnov said he hoped a new government would enable the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) to complete its term in office.

He said that in early January his outgoing cabinet would submit to parliament a package of economic measures including a draft 1997 budget, a new privatisation law and measures for the introduction of a currency board fixed exchange rate regime, allowing parliament to vote on them by mid-January.
A vote was expected later on Saturday. If the resignation is approved the party will nominate a new prime minister.

The leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), Ivan Kostov, attacked the government's record and said he regretted that Videnov had preferred to resign rather than negotiate with the opposition.
"The resignation of the cabinet is a belated admission of the failure of the BSP," Kostov said.
Stefan Savov, leader of the UDF-allied People's Union, accused the Socialists of trying to return to the communist era of former hardline leader Todor Zhivkov.

"The BSP is in no condition to make change. This is the tragedy of a people which you have made beggars," he told Videnov. "There is only one way out of the crisis and that is early parliamentary elections. You don't need them but the people do."
On Tuesday, the Socialist congress elected Georgi Parvanov as party leader, a choice seen as a compromise between party reformists and hardliners.

Possible prime ministers include the speaker of parliament Blagovest Sendov, seen as a compromise candidate, and former foreign minister Georgi Pirinski, who resigned after a party confidence vote gave Videnov only narrow backing last month.

The BSP was formed by leading ex-communists who renamed the party after Zhivkov's overthrow in 1989. Its critics accuse it of being more interested in supporting its powerful business allies than in pushing through badly-needed economic reforms.
Yuzhel Atilla of the ethnic Turkish Movement for Rights and Freedoms accused the Socialists of siphoning money abroad. "Billions of dollars left the country secretly," he said.

Videnov's government is half way through its four-year term. Failure to carry out reforms such as closing loss-making state firms has led to suspension of funding from the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, who support the currency board as a last chance to save the economy from disaster.
